text: SQS visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds and can be set from 0 seconds to 12 hours; a worker can extend it mid-processing with ChangeMessageVisibility (a 'heartbeat'), but never past 12 hours from first receipt.
why: Gives the actual default/limits behind the teacher's example values.

text: SQS retries are not infinite unless you let them be: a redrive policy's maxReceiveCount moves a message to a dead-letter queue after that many failed receives.
why: Poison messages otherwise circulate forever.

text: SQS standard queues are at-least-once: 'more than one copy of a message might be delivered' and order is best-effort, even within the visibility timeout. Make consumers idempotent.
why: Directly affects the total_blogs++ example.

text: SQS FIFO queues preserve order per MessageGroupId: while one message of a group is in flight, later messages of that group are held back. They also deduplicate (exactly-once processing).
why: Per-entity ordering is available on SQS, not only on Kinesis/Kafka.

text: SQS consumers pull with ReceiveMessage; long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 s) waits for messages and cuts empty responses and cost.
why: Practical detail for pull-based queue consumers.

text: RabbitMQ is the opposite: consumers normally subscribe and the broker pushes messages to them; polling with basic.get is 'highly discouraged'.
why: Corrects the 'queues are never push-based' generalisation.

text: RabbitMQ Streams (introduced in 3.9, 2021) are an append-only, replicated log with non-destructive reads; consumers can start from the beginning, an offset or a timestamp.
why: Names the actual RabbitMQ feature for stream use cases.

text: Kafka's broker default retention is 7 days (log.retention.hours=168, no size limit). Topics can instead use log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact), which keeps the latest record per key.
why: 'Persisted almost forever' is a config choice, not the default.

text: Kinesis keeps records for 24 hours by default, extendable to 365 days at extra cost.
why: Retention differs sharply from Kafka's default.

text: Each provisioned Kinesis shard handles up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes and 2 MB/s of reads (5 GetRecords calls/s); shard count sets both throughput and consumer parallelism.
why: Gives concrete shard sizing numbers.

text: Kinesis shard-to-worker assignment is done by the Kinesis Client Library using a DynamoDB lease table (one worker holds each shard's lease at a time); that table is billed to you.
why: Clarifies who manages assignment in Kinesis.

text: Kafka 4.0 added 'Queues for Kafka' share groups as early access; Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026) made them production-ready. A share group can have more consumers than partitions, with per-record acknowledgements, but without per-partition ordering.
why: The partition-count ceiling no longer applies to all Kafka consumption.

text: Kafka 4.0 made the KIP-848 consumer group protocol GA: assignment moves to the broker and 'stop-the-world' rebalances go away. Clients opt in with group.protocol=consumer (default is still classic in 4.2).
why: Version-dependent rebalancing behaviour.

text: Adding partitions doesn't move existing data, and keyed records may start going to a different partition, which 'may disturb consumers' relying on it. Kafka cannot reduce a topic's partition count.
why: Partition count is hard to change later.

text: Records with no key don't get hashed: the default producer uses a 'sticky' partition and switches after about batch.size bytes.
why: Completes the partitioning picture.

text: Producer-side ordering within a partition relies on idempotence (enable.idempotence=true by default). With idempotence off and more than 1 in-flight request, retries can reorder records.
why: Ordering guarantee has a producer-side precondition.

text: Kafka's docs: at-least-once by default; at-most-once by committing before processing; exactly-once via transactional producers + read_committed consumers for Kafka-to-Kafka processing. Exactly-once into external systems 'generally requires cooperation' from them.
why: Precise statement of Kafka's delivery semantics.

text: enable.auto.commit defaults to true with a 5 s interval. It gives at-least-once only if you finish processing each poll() batch before the next poll; otherwise records can be skipped.
why: Explains 'commits nobody wrote' and the trap in auto-commit.

text: A Kafka consumer's position per partition is one integer (the next offset to read), so it is cheap to checkpoint, and a consumer can rewind to an older offset to reprocess data.
why: Explains why commits are cheap and replay is possible.

text: Pricing dimensions: SQS bills per request, each 64 KB of payload counting as one request (1M requests/month free). Kinesis provisioned bills per shard-hour plus PUT payload units; on-demand bills per GB in/out plus a per-stream hourly fee.
why: Grounds the cost comparison.

text: SNS FIFO topics can archive messages for 1 to 365 days and replay them to subscriptions, narrowing the replay gap between SNS+SQS and Kafka.
why: Version-dependent AWS capability.

text: When a service must both update its DB and publish an event, the transactional outbox pattern writes the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction and a relay publishes it, avoiding 2PC. Consumers must still be idempotent.
why: Standard alternative to distributed transactions.

text: Elasticsearch search is near real-time: indexes refresh every 1 s by default (only on indices searched in the last 30 s), so a newly indexed blog may not be searchable instantly.
why: Adds latency expectation for the search consumer.

text: PostgreSQL's default isolation is READ COMMITTED. UPDATE ... SET claps = claps + 1 applies to the latest committed row version, so concurrent claps aren't lost; read-then-write in application code needs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a stricter isolation level.
why: Makes the clap-counter guidance safe.

text: A semaphore 'initialized to one' (a binary semaphore) acts as a mutual-exclusion lock; for a plain counter, an atomic increment such as Java's AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() needs no lock at all.
why: Shows the precise primitive and the lock-free alternative.
